topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: In every phase of operation, the loading, mass and CG must comply with the limits in which document?

options.text: The aeroplane's type certificate data sheet only
The flight manual, or Operations Manual if stricter
The load sheet prepared for the previous flight
The Operations Manual only, even where it is less restrictive

explanation: The aeroplane must stay within the limits of the approved flight manual, or of the Operations Manual where that is more restrictive. The stricter of the two always wins.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Who must be satisfied that the aeroplane's loading, mass and CG are within limits before flight?

options.text: The airport handling agent
The operator's maintenance department
The loading supervisor
The commander

explanation: Others prepare and supervise the load, but the commander carries the responsibility of satisfying himself or herself that the limits are met.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: What is the main purpose of the limits placed on aeroplane mass?

options.text: To keep adequate stability and control
To limit the cost of landing fees
To protect strength and performance
To limit noise on the ground

explanation: Mass limits protect structural strength and performance. CG limits are the ones that protect stability and control.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: What is the main purpose of the limits placed on CG position?

options.text: To keep stability and control
To reduce the fuel consumption in the cruise
To keep adequate margins of structural strength in flight
To keep the take-off distance short

explanation: CG limits ensure the aeroplane remains stable and controllable. Strength and performance are what the mass limits protect.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: In mass and balance work, how are "mass" and "weight" treated?

options.text: Mass applies on the ground and weight in flight
As meaning the same thing
Mass is used for fuel and weight for passengers
Weight is mass multiplied by the load factor

explanation: Mass and balance texts use the two words interchangeably. Only in a weighing calculation in newtons must weight be divided by g to give mass.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: What is structural fatigue in this context?

options.text: The bending of a part that springs back when unloaded
The loss of strength caused only by corrosion
A permanent loss of material properties
A temporary loss of strength that recovers when the part rests

explanation: Fatigue is a permanent loss of properties such as strength, durability and hardness. It is cumulative and cannot be reversed, and if undetected it can end in structural failure.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Which statement about structural fatigue is correct?

options.text: It is cumulative and cannot be reversed
It occurs only above the design ultimate load
It disappears after each major maintenance check
It is caused only by extreme temperatures

explanation: Fatigue builds up over the life of the structure and is not reversible. Extra fatigue from overloading can make a part fail earlier than predicted.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Which factor is described as the principal cause of fatigue in an aircraft structure?

options.text: Inappropriate use by pilots
Age of the airframe
Hot and humid climates
Weight

explanation: Age, inappropriate use and harsh environments all add fatigue, but weight is the principal stress factor, which is why overloading is so harmful.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Which kinds of stress do the four forces in flight induce in the structure?

options.text: Bending and shear only
Torsion only, about the wing root and the tail
Tension, compression, torsion, bending
Tension and compression only

explanation: Lift, weight, thrust and drag load the structural members in tension, compression, torsion and bending, often while the structure also sees large temperature changes.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: What is the design limit load (DLL)?

options.text: The most load allowed repeatedly in normal use
The load that causes visible permanent deformation
The load at which the structure is expected to collapse
The minimum load the structure must absorb in an emergency

explanation: The DLL is the maximum load that can be applied repeatedly in normal operation without excessive fatigue. A pilot must never deliberately exceed it.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: How is the design ultimate load (DUL) obtained from the design limit load?

options.text: By adding a 15% factor of safety
By doubling the design limit load
By adding a 25% factor of safety
By adding a 50% factor of safety

explanation: The authorities impose a factor of safety of 50%, so the DUL is 1.5 times the DLL. It is the minimum load the structure must absorb in an emergency without collapsing.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: What is the design ultimate load?

options.text: The load used to set the maximum zero fuel mass
The least load it must take in an emergency
The load at which fatigue starts to accumulate
The greatest load that may be applied repeatedly in normal operation

explanation: The DUL is the minimum load the structure must withstand in an emergency, such as a heavy landing or extreme gusts, without collapsing. Loads above it are likely to cause permanent damage or collapse.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: The design limit load of a member is 40 kN. What is its design ultimate load?

options.text: 80 kN
50 kN
46 kN
60 kN

explanation: The DUL is the DLL plus 50%: 40 × 1.5 = 60 kN. Doubling (80 kN) or adding 25% (50 kN) uses the wrong factor.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Why are aircraft structures made only just strong enough for the design ultimate load?

options.text: To allow the limit load to be exceeded safely
To keep the structural weight to a minimum
So that fatigue cannot accumulate
Because stronger materials cannot be certified

explanation: Every kilogram of structure is a kilogram less payload, so materials are chosen to be only just capable of absorbing the DUL.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Which structural mass limits does the manufacturer set to protect the airframe?

options.text: Taxi, zero fuel, take-off, landing
Traffic load and useful load
Trip fuel and reserve fuel masses
Basic empty mass and dry operating mass only

explanation: The manufacturer imposes the maximum taxi mass, maximum zero fuel mass, maximum structural take-off mass and maximum structural landing mass, which must never be exceeded in normal operation.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: How does an increase in aeroplane mass affect V1, VR and V2?

options.text: V1 increases but VR and V2 do not change
They do not change, because they are IAS values
All three increase
All three decrease

explanation: A heavier aeroplane needs more lift, so all take-off speeds rise, as does the distance needed to stop.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: How does increased mass affect climb performance?

options.text: Only the ceiling reduces; climb rates do not change
Rate of climb reduces but the ceiling increases
Climb gradient increases because of greater inertia
Gradient, rate and ceiling all reduce

explanation: More weight means less excess thrust and power relative to weight, so the gradient, the rate of climb and the ceiling all decrease.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: With an increase in mass, what happens to the stalling speed and the maximum speed?

options.text: Stalling speed falls; maximum speed rises
Both rise
Stalling speed rises; maximum speed falls
Both fall

explanation: A heavier aeroplane stalls at a higher speed and, because drag is greater, reaches a lower maximum speed, so the usable speed range shrinks.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: What happens to the margin between low-speed and high-speed buffet as mass increases?

options.text: It decreases
It increases at high altitude only
It is unchanged; only altitude affects it
It increases

explanation: Higher mass raises the low-speed buffet speed, so the effective speed range between low- and high-speed buffet, and the safety margin, reduce.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: What effect does increased mass have on range and endurance?

options.text: Neither changes; only fuel load matters
Both decrease
Both increase
Range reduces but endurance increases

explanation: More mass means more drag and higher fuel consumption, so both range and endurance fall.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Which effect does an increase in mass have on the aeroplane's handling?

options.text: Manoeuvrability reduces
It becomes more responsive in pitch
Handling is unaffected below the maximum mass
Stick forces become very light

explanation: A heavier aeroplane is less responsive to control inputs and more difficult to fly.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Which of these increases with aeroplane mass?

options.text: Maximum level flight speed at all altitudes
Rate of climb
Maximum altitude
Braking energy

explanation: Increased mass raises braking energy, tyre and brake wear, undercarriage loads, wing root stress and structural fatigue, while maximum altitude, rate of climb and maximum speed all reduce.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: How does increased mass affect the rate of descent?

options.text: It decreases
It increases
It is unchanged
It decreases only in a glide

explanation: For the same configuration a heavier aeroplane descends faster, because it flies faster along the same gradient.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Which statement describes the centre of gravity?

options.text: The point through which the total lift acts
The point at the quarter chord of the wing
Where the total weight acts
The point where the datum is located

explanation: The CG is the point through which the whole weight is said to act. It is the balance point, the point the aeroplane manoeuvres about and the point through which its three axes pass.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: About which point does an aeroplane manoeuvre in flight?

options.text: The datum
The centre of gravity
The centre of pressure
The aerodynamic centre

explanation: The CG is the point the aircraft rotates about in the air and the point through which the three axes pass, which is why its position governs stability.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: As the CG moves forward from the middle of its range, what happens to stability and manoeuvrability?

options.text: Stability decreases; manoeuvrability increases
Both increase
Both decrease
Stability increases; manoeuvrability decreases

explanation: A forward CG makes the aeroplane progressively more stable and less manoeuvrable; an aft CG does the opposite.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: What is the danger of too much stability from a far forward CG?

options.text: High control forces and pilot workload
A lower stalling speed than expected
A tendency to enter a flat spin
Light stick forces and easy over-stressing

explanation: Too much stability raises the stick forces the pilot must overcome. Light stick forces and flat spins belong to an aft CG.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Which causes the CG to move during flight?

options.text: Changes in airspeed only
Changes in outside air temperature only
Fuel burn, flaps and people moving
The aerodynamic centre moving with speed

explanation: The CG is not fixed: it moves with fuel consumption, flap position and crew and passenger movement. The operator must ensure it stays within the limits.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Who is responsible for keeping the CG movement within the manufacturer's limits?

options.text: The cabin crew only
The manufacturer
The aerodrome operator
The operator

explanation: The manufacturer sets the CG limits; the operator must ensure the CG stays within them throughout operation.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Why does the manufacturer set CG limits?

options.text: To keep the landing gear loads equal
To make the aeroplane as fuel efficient as is possible in cruise
So an average pilot can fly it with normal effort
To make the aeroplane as manoeuvrable as possible

explanation: The CG range is set so that an average pilot can control the aeroplane safely through all stages of flight with normal piloting effort and without fatigue.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: When must the CG be within its limits?

options.text: At all times, airborne or on the ground
Only at take-off and landing
Only at the zero fuel mass
Only in flight

explanation: The CG must stay within limits at all times, including loading and unloading on the ground. Expected changes during the flight must be accounted for before take-off.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: In mass and balance, what is a "couple"?

options.text: The sum of all moments about the datum
Two forces acting together to produce turning
A mass and its balance arm
Two forces of equal size in the same direction

explanation: A couple is two forces acting together to produce a turning motion, such as lift and weight acting at different points along the fuselage.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Why does a CG forward of the limit increase drag?

options.text: The wing must fly at a smaller angle of attack
The tailplane must make a larger down load
The fuselage flies nose-down
The ailerons must be held deflected

explanation: The nose-down moment must be balanced by a tail down load. The elevator deflection and tail lift add drag, raising fuel consumption and reducing range and endurance.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Why does the stalling speed rise with a CG forward of the limit?

options.text: The tail down force acts like extra weight
The aeroplane flies at a lower angle of attack
The centre of pressure moves aft
The wing's maximum lift coefficient falls

explanation: The extra tail down force must be carried by the wing, so the wing must produce more lift, as if the aeroplane were heavier. The stall speed and take-off and landing speeds rise.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: With the CG forward of the limit, what happens to V1, VR and VMU?

options.text: VR decreases but V1 increases
They do not change
They increase
They decrease

explanation: On the ground the aeroplane rotates about its main wheels. A more forward CG gives a larger nose-down force the elevator must overcome, so more airflow and a higher speed are needed to rotate.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: How does a CG forward of the limit affect the ability to pitch the aeroplane?

options.text: The aeroplane becomes unstable in pitch
It is unchanged in flight but better on the ground
Pitch control is increased
Pitch control is reduced

explanation: The greater stability reduces the ability to pitch the nose up or down, which can be critical during rotation and the landing flare.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: How does a CG forward of the limit affect the safe speed range?

options.text: It widens, and the buffet margin increases
It narrows, and the buffet margin reduces
It is unchanged
It widens at high altitude only

explanation: The higher stall speed reduces the available speed range and narrows the margin between low- and high-speed buffet.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: What is the main danger of a CG aft of the limit?

options.text: Low stability, light stick forces
High stick forces leading to pilot fatigue
A higher stalling speed
Higher take-off speeds

explanation: With the CG too far aft the aeroplane becomes unstable in pitch and stick forces are light, so the pilot may over-stress it by applying too much g.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Why is an aft CG beyond the limit dangerous in a spin?

options.text: The aeroplane cannot enter a fully developed spin
The spin becomes steeper and faster
Spin recovery needs less rudder
A flat spin is more likely

explanation: An aft CG makes a flat spin more likely and recovery more difficult.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: With the CG aft of the limit, why may the glide angle be harder to hold?

options.text: The wing stalls at a lower angle of attack
The elevator loses all effectiveness
The aeroplane tends to pitch up
The aeroplane tends to pitch down

explanation: The aft CG gives a pitch-up tendency, so a steady glide is harder to sustain.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Why may range decrease even with the CG aft of the limit, although an aft CG normally reduces drag?

options.text: Drag from extreme control inputs
The tailplane must produce a larger down load
The stalling speed rises
Fuel consumption rises at an aft CG

explanation: Within limits an aft CG reduces trim drag, but beyond the limit the constant extreme manoeuvres to control the unstable aeroplane add drag and are likely to reduce range and endurance.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Compared with the aft limit, which is true with the CG on the forward limit?

options.text: Better range and lower rotation speed
Higher stall speed and higher fuel consumption
Lighter stick forces and better climb gradient
Lower stall speed and lower fuel consumption

explanation: At the forward limit stability, stick forces, drag, stall speed, VR and fuel consumption are higher, and range, climb gradient and manoeuvrability are lower than at the aft limit.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: With the CG on the aft limit rather than the forward limit, what happens to the achievable climb gradient?

options.text: It decreases
It is unchanged
It increases
It increases only with flaps extended

explanation: An aft CG needs less tail down load, so drag and effective weight are lower and the climb gradient (and glide performance) is better.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: Which pair describes the CG on the aft limit compared with the forward limit?

options.text: Range up, stability up
Range down, stability up
Range down, stability down
Range up, stability down

explanation: Moving the CG aft improves range and reduces fuel consumption, but reduces stability and stick forces.

topic: 02 Limitations and Effects of Mass and CG
question: An aeroplane with its CG close to the forward limit is compared with the same aeroplane at the aft limit. Which effect follows?

options.text: A better rate of climb capability at all masses
Lower specific fuel consumption
A lower rate of climb
Less induced drag

explanation: A forward CG increases the tail down load, effectively adding weight and drag, so climb performance is worse and fuel consumption higher.
